 Repo rate hike: RBI’s tightrope walk between growth and inflation 
 Representational image 
 By Purna Chandra Padhan and Benudhar Sahu 
 Published October 29, 2026
 Spotify
 On October 7, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) increased the repo rate by 25 basis points, from 5.25% to 5.50%. The decision followed a comprehensive assessment of evolving macroeconomic conditions, global developments, and the economic outlook. The Standing Deposit Facility rate rose 5.25%, while the Marginal Standing Facility rate and the Bank Rate increased to 5.75%.
 The RBI also changed its policy stance from “neutral” to “calibrated tightening” to contain inflation while supporting sustainable economic growth. The ‘calibrated’ approach indicates a more measured approach to monetary tightening, with future rate decisions depending on expected inflation and evolving economic conditions.
 Why policy rate hike 
 RBI’s tightening measures came amid rising food and energy prices, weather-related disruptions, and higher crude oil prices. Inflationary pressure was a key concern. India’s retail inflation, measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI), rose to 4.82% in August 2026, up from 4.45% in July. Food inflation, measured by the Consumer Food Price Index (CFPI), also increased to 5.95% from 5.52% (see Exhibit 1). Retail inflation remained above the RBI’s medium-term target of 4% for a third consecutive month. Persistent inflation strengthened expectations of tighter monetary policy for longer.
 Climate and geopolitical risk 
 Weather-related risks further worsened the inflation outlook. Flood and drought-like conditions across many states threatened food supply, while the possibility of El Niño conditions extending into 2027 added uncertainty. Global economic developments and geopolitical tensions also intensified inflationary pressure. The Russia-Ukraine war and the West Asia conflict added unpredictability to the global economic prospect.
 Amid these tensions, crude oil prices rose above $100 per barrel, raising concerns about India’s external balance. Higher crude prices could widen the current account deficit, weaken the rupee, and increase the import bill. Rising energy costs could also push up manufacturing, logistics, and transportation expenses, ultimately fueling domestic inflation.
 International bond market tightening 
 In September, global monetary tightening intensified pressure on India’s financial markets. The US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4%, marking its first-rate hike since July 2023, while US 10-year Treasury yields climbed by 53 basis points to 5.3% over the month. In India, the benchmark 10-year government bond yield rose by 25 basis points to 7.21%, signaling broader upward pressure on borrowing costs. The narrowing interest-rate differential between India and the US put additional pressure on the rupee and domestic financial markets.
 These developments, coupled with global trade uncertainty and elevated crude prices, complicated the RBI’s policy decisions. High global yields could increase pressure on the RBI to raise the repo rate to contain inflation risks and support the rupee.
 Pressure on economic growth 
 The repo rate hike is expected to affect households, businesses, and India’s economic growth. It may increase lending rates, especially for loans linked to external benchmarks. As a result, borrowers may face higher EMIs on personal, home, and vehicle loans. This could reduce disposable income and discretionary spending.
 Higher interest rates may raise borrowing costs for businesses. This could delay their investment and expansion plans. NBFCs may also face higher funding costs. However, banks may attract people to save more by offering better interest rates on fixed deposits.
 Higher borrowing costs may slow investment, job creation, and economic growth. Sectors such as real estate and manufacturing may face greater pressure. In the real estate sector, home buyers and developers may adopt a cautious approach. However, the premium housing segment is likely to remain resilient. Strong market fundamentals, changing lifestyle preferences, and improved buyer confidence may continue to support demand.
 Growth trajectory 
 India’s economy grew by 7.8% in the first quarter of FY2027. Rising consumption, investment, and exports supported this growth. Bank credit, GST collections, and automobile sales also remained healthy. Despite external shocks, the Indian economy continues to demonstrate resilience.
 Foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows reached $13.8 billion between April and August 2026. Foreign exchange reserves stood at $734.6 billion, providing nearly 11 months of import cover. However, foreign portfolio investment witnessed new outflows. The overall balance of payments (BoP) is expected to record a substantial surplus in FY 2026-27. The banking sector continues to record broad-based credit growth. Scheduled commercial banks and NBFCs remain strong in terms of asset quality, capital adequacy, and profitability. These factors provide a solid foundation for the financial system.
 Strong domestic growth has given the RBI some room to tighten monetary policy. Higher interest rates can help moderate demand and prevent inflation from becoming entrenched. The RBI has also raised its FY 2026-27 real GDP growth forecast to 7.1%, up from the earlier estimate of 6.7%. Strong domestic demand, investment, and consumption support this outlook.
 Other institutions also predict India to maintain healthy growth. The OECD projects growth at 7.1% for FY 2026-27. The Asian Development Bank, S&P Global Ratings, and Moody’s project growth at around 7%. Fitch maintains a more cautious forecast of 6.9%. Despite external challenges, the RBI has expressed confidence in the domestic economy. The services sector continues to benefit from steady domestic and international demand. Manufacturing activity also remains firm despite rising cost pressures.
 The repo rate hike signals the RBI’s focus on controlling inflation and maintaining macroeconomic stability. However, higher borrowing costs may create challenges for micro and small enterprises. First-generation entrepreneurs, in particular, may struggle with rising operational costs and limited access to affordable credit. This could affect their expansion plans and long-term growth.
 The RBI’s policy dilemma 
 The RBI faces a difficult choice between controlling inflation and sustaining economic growth. Further rate hikes or a prolonged pause will depend on inflation trends and changing macroeconomic dynamics. RBI has ruled out near-term rate cuts amid rising crude oil and food prices.
 Markets are anticipating three interest rate hikes by February 2027, potentially increasing borrowing costs by 75 basis points. Meanwhile, economists have cautioned that El Niño conditions could intensify inflationary pressures and weigh on economic growth in 2027.
 Higher interest rates can help control inflation. However, they also raise borrowing costs and may reduce consumption and investment. Tighter global financial conditions could add to these challenges. The RBI must therefore ensure that inflation comes under control without significantly slowing economic growth.
 Path ahead 
 Given the global economic uncertainties, the RBI needs to choose a narrow path between price stability and avoiding a growth slowdown. It should closely monitor food prices, monsoon conditions, crude oil trends, and inflation expectations before planning future policy decisions. An extended pause in rate hikes may be necessary if inflation shows signs of easing, while further hikes may be required if price pressures persist.
 The government’s fiscal policy measures, such as subsidies, welfare spending, and support for MSMEs, can help complement monetary tightening and reduce the adverse impacts of rate hikes on vulnerable households and sectors. Other measures to reduce supply-side bottlenecks and improve food supply can help contain inflation despite the higher interest rates.
 Thus, the key challenge before RBI in the coming days is to adopt a balanced approach to inflation control and sustainable economic growth.
